molecules.name: Hydrogen
notes: The simplest covalent bond: two 1s orbitals overlap end-on to make one σ bond.
Bond length 74 pm, bond energy 436 kJ/mol. Diamagnetic (σ1s² in MO theory), bond order 1.

molecules.name: Oxygen
notes: O=O: one σ and one π bond; bond length 121 pm, bond order 2.
Paramagnetic: two unpaired electrons sit in the π*2p orbitals. Lewis structures cannot show this, but molecular orbital theory does.

molecules.name: Nitrogen
notes: N≡N: one σ and two π bonds; bond length 110 pm, bond order 3, bond energy 946 kJ/mol.
Diamagnetic and very inert because of the strong triple bond. Isoelectronic with CO, CN⁻ and NO⁺.

molecules.name: Hydrogen chloride
notes: Polar covalent: Cl is more electronegative, so H carries δ⁺ and Cl carries δ⁻. Dipole moment ≈ 1.08 D.
Bond length 127 pm. Dipole moment = charge × distance (μ = q × d).

molecules.name: Carbon monoxide
notes: C≡O has one σ and two π bonds; one of the π bonds is a coordinate (dative) bond from O to C.
Isoelectronic with N₂ and CN⁻, bond order 3, bond length 113 pm. Toxic because it binds haemoglobin about 200× more strongly than O₂.

molecules.name: Water
notes: Four electron pairs (2 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs) → tetrahedral arrangement, bent shape.
Lone pair–lone pair repulsion > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair, so the angle shrinks from 109.5° to 104.5°.
Strongly polar (1.85 D) and forms hydrogen bonds, which explains its high boiling point.

molecules.name: Hydrogen sulfide
notes: Bond angle trend down the group: H₂O 104.5° > H₂S 92° > H₂Se 91° > H₂Te 90°.
S is larger and less electronegative than O, so bond pairs sit farther from S and repel less; S uses nearly pure p orbitals.

molecules.name: Ammonia
notes: 3 bond pairs + 1 lone pair: the lone pair pushes the N–H bonds closer, so 107° instead of 109.5°.
Dipole moment 1.47 D. In NF₃ it is only 0.23 D because the N–F bond dipoles oppose the lone-pair dipole.
Compare: PH₃ 93.5°, AsH₃ 91.8°. Angle falls down the group.

molecules.name: Methane
notes: Four equivalent σ(sp³–s) bonds, C–H 109 pm, all angles 109.5°.
Non-polar because the four bond dipoles cancel by symmetry.

molecules.name: Boron trifluoride
notes: Electron-deficient: boron has only 6 electrons, so BF₃ is a Lewis acid (it accepts a pair, forming BF₄⁻ with sp³ B).
B–F bond (130 pm) is shorter than expected because of pπ–pπ back-bonding from F lone pairs. Lewis acidity: BBr₃ > BCl₃ > BF₃.

molecules.name: Beryllium chloride (gas)
notes: Gas-phase monomer is linear and sp-hybridised. Be has only 4 electrons in the valence shell (electron-deficient).
In the solid state it forms a chain polymer with bridging Cl atoms.

molecules.name: Carbon dioxide
notes: 2 σ + 2 π bonds; C=O 116 pm (shorter than a normal C=O, ~121 pm).
Each C=O bond is polar but the dipoles cancel, so the molecule is non-polar.

molecules.name: Sulfur dioxide
notes: 2 bond pairs + 1 lone pair on S: bent. Both S–O bonds are identical (resonance).
Polar (1.63 D); acidic oxide, bleaches by reduction, causes acid rain.

molecules.name: Sulfur trioxide
notes: Three equivalent S–O bonds (resonance), S–O 142 pm.
Non-polar, strongly acidic oxide: SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄.

molecules.name: Ozone
notes: Two equivalent O–O bonds of 128 pm (between a single 148 pm and a double 121 pm): resonance hybrid, bond order 1.5.
Polar even though all atoms are the same: the central O is positive and the end O atoms share the negative charge.

molecules.name: Phosphorus trichloride
notes: One lone pair on P compresses the Cl–P–Cl angle to about 100°.
Hydrolyses in water to H₃PO₃ and HCl.

molecules.name: Phosphorus pentachloride
notes: Two axial P–Cl bonds (219 pm) are longer than the three equatorial ones (204 pm) because of greater repulsion from the 3 equatorial pairs.
Non-polar overall. In the solid state it is ionic: [PCl₄]⁺[PCl₆]⁻.

molecules.name: Sulfur tetrafluoride
notes: The lone pair sits in an equatorial position (minimum repulsion), giving the see-saw shape.
4 bond pairs + 1 lone pair: AX₄E.

molecules.name: Chlorine trifluoride
notes: Both lone pairs occupy equatorial positions, leaving a T shape (AX₃E₂).
Same shape as BrF₃. Compare with BF₃ (trigonal planar, no lone pair).

molecules.name: Xenon difluoride
notes: Three lone pairs lie in the equatorial plane (AX₂E₃), so the two F atoms are axial and linear.
Non-polar. Isoelectronic and isostructural with I₃⁻ and ICl₂⁻.

molecules.name: Sulfur hexafluoride
notes: Six equivalent S–F bonds, all angles 90° (and 180° across).
Chemically inert (F atoms shield S); a greenhouse gas used as an insulator in switchgear.

molecules.name: Bromine pentafluoride
notes: 5 bond pairs + 1 lone pair (AX₅E): the lone pair sits trans to the apical F, and the four basal F atoms bend slightly toward the apical F (84.8° instead of 90°).
Same shape as XeOF₄ and IF₅.

molecules.name: Xenon tetrafluoride
notes: Two lone pairs occupy the axial positions, trans to each other (AX₄E₂), leaving a planar square of F atoms.
Non-polar. Prepared by heating Xe and F₂ (1 : 5) at 873 K and 7 bar: Xe + 2F₂ → XeF₄.

molecules.name: Iodine heptafluoride
notes: 7 bond pairs: 5 equatorial (72° apart) and 2 axial (90° to the plane). The only common sp³d³ example.
Non-polar by symmetry; I is in the +7 oxidation state.

molecules.name: Xenon trioxide
notes: Xe is in the +6 state; isostructural with ClO₃⁻ and SO₃²⁻ (pyramidal, one lone pair).
Dangerously explosive solid. Formed by hydrolysis of XeF₆.

molecules.name: Xenon tetroxide
notes: Xe is in the +8 state, isoelectronic with IO₄⁻ and isostructural with ClO₄⁻. Unstable and explosive.

molecules.name: Xenon oxytetrafluoride
notes: Xe is +6: 4 Xe–F bonds, one Xe=O and one lone pair (AX₅E), exactly like BrF₅ in shape.
Made by partial hydrolysis of XeF₆.

molecules.name: Hydrogen cyanide
notes: C is sp-hybridised: 2 σ bonds + 2 π bonds (C≡N). Weak acid (pKa 9.2); very poisonous.

molecules.name: Nitrous oxide
notes: Laughing gas. Resonance between N≡N⁺–O⁻ and ⁻N=N⁺=O. Central N is sp-hybridised; isoelectronic with CO₂.
Asymmetric (N–N–O), so slightly polar.

molecules.name: Hydrogen peroxide
notes: The two O–H bonds lie in two planes like the pages of a half-open book; the dihedral angle is 111.5° in the gas phase and 90.2° in the solid.
O–O single bond 147 pm; oxidation state of O is −1. Acts as both oxidising and reducing agent.

molecules.name: Hydronium ion
notes: H⁺ attached to a water lone pair by a coordinate bond. This is what "H⁺(aq)" really is.
Isoelectronic with NH₃ and, like it, pyramidal with sp³ O.

molecules.name: Ammonium ion
notes: Formed when NH₃ uses its lone pair to bond to H⁺ (coordinate bond). All four N–H bonds are identical.
Isoelectronic and isostructural with CH₄.

molecules.name: Nitrate ion
notes: Three equivalent N–O bonds (resonance), bond order 1.33, N–O ≈ 124 pm.
Isoelectronic with CO₃²⁻. The brown-ring test for nitrate gives [Fe(H₂O)₅NO]²⁺.

molecules.name: Nitrite ion
notes: One lone pair on N bends the ion; both N–O bonds equal (bond order 1.5). Isoelectronic with O₃.

molecules.name: Carbonate ion
notes: Resonance among three structures; each C–O has bond order 1.33 and length 129 pm.
Isoelectronic with NO₃⁻.

molecules.name: Sulfite ion
notes: S has 3 bond pairs and 1 lone pair, so it is pyramidal (unlike planar SO₃).
Isostructural with ClO₃⁻ and XeO₃.

molecules.name: Sulfate ion
notes: All four S–O bonds are equivalent (bond order 1.5, 149 pm) through resonance.
Isostructural with PO₄³⁻, ClO₄⁻ and CrO₄²⁻.

molecules.name: Phosphate ion
notes: Bond order 1.25: one double bond shared by four P–O bonds. Conjugate base of H₃PO₄ (after losing all three H⁺).

molecules.name: Chlorate ion
notes: Cl(+5): 3 bond pairs + 1 lone pair, pyramidal. Compare ClO₄⁻, which is tetrahedral with no lone pair.

molecules.name: Perchlorate ion
notes: Four identical Cl–O bonds (bond order 1.75). Cl is +7. Very stable and a very weak base (conjugate base of the strongest oxoacid, HClO₄).

molecules.name: Triiodide ion
notes: Formed when I₂ dissolves in KI solution (I₂ + I⁻ → I₃⁻), giving a brown solution; the starch–iodine blue colour is due to I₃⁻.
Central I has 3 lone pairs in the equatorial plane, exactly like XeF₂ (isoelectronic).

molecules.name: Permanganate ion
notes: Mn is +7 (d⁰), so the deep purple colour is charge transfer (O → Mn), not d–d. It is diamagnetic.
Strong oxidising agent: in acid Mn(+7) → Mn²⁺ (5 e⁻); in neutral medium → MnO₂ (3 e⁻).

molecules.name: Chromate ion
notes: Yellow, Cr(+6). In acid it condenses to orange dichromate: 2CrO₄²⁻ + 2H⁺ ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻ + H₂O.

molecules.name: Dichromate ion
molecules.shape: Two tetrahedra sharing a corner O
notes: Two CrO₄ tetrahedra joined through one bridging O (Cr–O–Cr ≈ 126°); 6 terminal Cr–O bonds are shorter (≈163 pm) than the bridging ones.
Orange; Cr is +6 throughout. In acid it oxidises Fe²⁺, I⁻, SO₃²⁻ and alcohols; Cr(+6) → Cr³⁺ (6 e⁻ per dichromate).

molecules.name: Nitric acid
notes: N is +5 and sp²-hybridised; the two terminal N–O bonds are equivalent by resonance (≈121 pm) and shorter than N–OH (141 pm).
Strong monobasic acid and a powerful oxidising agent. Nitrate (NO₃⁻) is planar.

molecules.name: Sulfuric acid
notes: S is +6 with 2 S=O (143 pm) and 2 S–OH (157 pm) bonds. Dibasic: two ionisable H atoms.
Strong dehydrating and oxidising agent (hot, conc.). Manufactured by the Contact process.

molecules.name: Phosphoric acid
notes: One P=O and three P–OH bonds; P is +5. Tribasic (3 ionisable H atoms). Used in fertilisers and cola drinks.
Its conjugate bases are H₂PO₄⁻, HPO₄²⁻ and PO₄³⁻.

molecules.name: Phosphorous acid
notes: P(+3) with one P–H, one P=O and two P–OH. Only the two O–H hydrogens ionise, so it is DIBASIC although it has three H atoms.
Disproportionates on heating: 4H₃PO₃ → 3H₃PO₄ + PH₃. A reducing agent.

molecules.name: Hypophosphorous acid
notes: P(+1) with two P–H, one P=O and one P–OH. Only ONE ionisable H, so it is monobasic.
Strong reducing agent (reduces Ag⁺ to Ag), because of the two P–H bonds.

molecules.name: Perchloric acid
notes: Cl is +7. The strongest common oxoacid, because ClO₄⁻ spreads its negative charge over four O atoms (most stable conjugate base).
Acid strength: HClO < HClO₂ < HClO₃ < HClO₄.

molecules.name: Boric acid
notes: B(OH)₃ is a weak MONOBASIC acid, not because it loses H⁺ but because it accepts OH⁻ (Lewis acid): B(OH)₃ + 2H₂O → [B(OH)₄]⁻ + H₃O⁺.
In the solid, molecules are joined by hydrogen bonds into planar layers, which makes it slippery.

molecules.name: Chromium pentoxide (chromium peroxide)
molecules.shape: Butterfly: one oxo + two side-on peroxo groups
notes: Cr is +6, not +10: the one oxide O (−2) and the two peroxide groups O₂²⁻ (−2 each) total −6, so Cr must be +6.
Contains two peroxy (O–O) linkages and one Cr=O bond: 1 Cr=O, 4 Cr–O, 2 O–O. Counting four O atoms as −2 each would wrongly give +10.
Blue colour (chromium peroxide test for H₂O₂ / chromate: blue in ether or amyl alcohol layer).

molecules.name: Diborane
molecules.shape: Two tetrahedra sharing an edge (banana bonds)
notes: 12 valence electrons for 8 bonds: 4 normal terminal B–H bonds (2c–2e) and 2 three-centre two-electron (3c–2e) "banana" bridge bonds.
Terminal B–H 119 pm are shorter than bridge B–H 133 pm. The two B and four terminal H lie in one plane; the bridging H atoms are above and below it.

molecules.name: Dinitrogen tetroxide
notes: Colourless dimer of brown NO₂ (2NO₂ ⇌ N₂O₄); N–N is very long and weak (178 pm).
Planar with N(+4) in each half; diamagnetic because the odd electrons of two NO₂ pair up.

molecules.name: White phosphorus
notes: Four P atoms at the corners of a tetrahedron: 6 P–P single bonds, one lone pair per P. The 60° angle is highly strained, so P₄ is very reactive (stored under water).
Red phosphorus is polymeric and much less reactive.

molecules.name: Phosphorus(III) oxide
notes: A tetrahedral P₄ skeleton with an O atom inserted into each of the six P–P bonds: 12 P–O bonds, 6 bridging O, each P keeps one lone pair.
Anhydride of H₃PO₃. P is in the +3 state.

molecules.name: Phosphorus(V) oxide
notes: P₄O₆ cage plus one terminal P=O on each P: 16 P–O bonds in all (12 P–O–P bridge bonds + 4 P=O). P is +5.
A powerful dehydrating agent; anhydride of H₃PO₄.

molecules.name: Octasulfur (rhombic sulfur)
notes: Eight S atoms in a non-planar crown ring; S–S 205 pm. Rhombic (α) and monoclinic (β) sulfur both contain S₈ rings and differ in how the rings pack.
Each S has 2 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs.

molecules.name: Aluminium chloride (dimer)
notes: AlCl₃ is electron-deficient (6 e⁻), so it dimerises: each bridging Cl uses a lone pair to form a coordinate bond to the other Al, completing the octet.
Terminal Al–Cl 206 pm vs bridging 221 pm. Above ~800 °C it dissociates to planar sp² AlCl₃. A Lewis acid (Friedel–Crafts catalyst).

molecules.name: Hexacyanoferrate(II) (ferrocyanide)
notes: Fe²⁺ is d⁶; strong-field CN⁻ pairs up the electrons (t₂g⁶), so the complex is low spin and DIAMAGNETIC. It uses d²sp³ (inner-orbital) hybridisation.
The ferricyanide [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ (Fe³⁺, d⁵) has one unpaired electron. Prussian blue is formed with Fe³⁺ / Fe²⁺ ions.

molecules.name: Hexaamminecobalt(III)
notes: Co³⁺ is d⁶; NH₃ is a strong-field ligand, so the electrons pair (t₂g⁶ e_g⁰): low spin, diamagnetic, inner-orbital complex. Orange-yellow.
Compare [CoF₆]³⁻: weak-field F⁻ gives a high-spin sp³d² complex with 4 unpaired electrons.

molecules.name: Tetracarbonylnickel(0)
notes: Ni(0) is 3d⁸4s² → 3d¹⁰ with CO (strong field, π-acceptor); sp³ hybridisation, diamagnetic. Used in the Mond process to purify nickel.
Metal carbonyl: CO donates a σ pair and Ni back-donates into CO π* (synergic bonding).

molecules.name: Tetrachloronickelate(II)
notes: Ni²⁺ is d⁸. Weak-field Cl⁻ does not pair the electrons, so it uses sp³ and is PARAMAGNETIC (2 unpaired e⁻).
Contrast with [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻: strong-field CN⁻ gives a diamagnetic square-planar dsp² complex.

molecules.name: Tetracyanonickelate(II)
notes: Ni²⁺ d⁸ with strong-field CN⁻: the 8 d electrons pair up, freeing one d orbital for dsp² hybridisation. Diamagnetic.

molecules.name: Tetrachloroplatinate(II)
notes: Pt²⁺ is d⁸. Heavy 5d metals strongly favour square-planar dsp² geometry, even with weak ligands like Cl⁻. Diamagnetic.

molecules.name: cis-Diamminedichloroplatinum(II) (cisplatin)
notes: Geometrical isomerism in a square-planar [MA₂B₂] complex: identical ligands adjacent = cis, opposite = trans.
The cis isomer is polar (μ ≠ 0) and is the anticancer drug cisplatin; the trans isomer (transplatin) is non-polar and inactive.

molecules.name: trans-Diamminedichloroplatinum(II)
notes: Trans isomer: identical ligands opposite each other, so the dipoles cancel (non-polar).

molecules.name: Tetraamminecopper(II)
notes: Cu²⁺ (d⁹) gives the deep blue colour seen when excess ammonia is added to Cu²⁺(aq). One unpaired electron, so paramagnetic.
NCERT treats it as dsp² square planar (the electron is promoted to 4p).

molecules.name: Diamminesilver(I) (Tollens’ reagent)
notes: Ag⁺ is d¹⁰ (diamagnetic) and forms linear sp complexes. Tollens’ reagent oxidises aldehydes, depositing a silver mirror.

molecules.name: trans-Dichlorotetraamminecobalt(III)
notes: Octahedral [MA₄B₂]: two Cl⁻ opposite each other = trans (green, "praseo" salt), non-polar.

molecules.name: cis-Dichlorotetraamminecobalt(III)
notes: The two Cl⁻ occupy adjacent corners (90° apart) = cis (violet, "violeo" salt); polar. Octahedral [MA₄B₂] shows only two geometrical isomers: cis and trans.

molecules.name: Ferrocene
notes: An organometallic "sandwich" compound: Fe²⁺ between two planar C₅H₅⁻ (Cp) rings, each donating 6 π electrons. 18-electron rule: 6 (Fe²⁺) + 12 = 18.
Diamagnetic and very stable; all five carbons of each ring bond to Fe (η⁵ bonding). Rings are eclipsed in the gas phase.

molecules.name: Ethane – staggered conformation
notes: Every C–H bond on one carbon sits midway between the C–H bonds on the other (dihedral 60°). This is the most stable conformation.
Rotation about C–C is nearly free (barrier ≈ 12 kJ/mol): the staggered and eclipsed forms interconvert millions of times per second.

molecules.name: Ethane – eclipsed conformation
notes: C–H bonds on the two carbons are directly in line (dihedral 0°). It is the least stable conformation: ≈ 12 kJ/mol (torsional strain) above the staggered form.
Torsional strain comes from repulsion between bonding electron pairs on adjacent carbons.

molecules.name: n-Butane – anti conformation
notes: The two CH₃ groups are 180° apart (dihedral C–C–C–C = 180°): the most stable conformer of butane.
Energy order: anti < gauche (+3.8 kJ/mol) < partially eclipsed < fully eclipsed.

molecules.name: n-Butane – gauche conformation
notes: The CH₃ groups are 60° apart. About 3.8 kJ/mol less stable than anti because of steric (van der Waals) repulsion.

molecules.name: n-Butane – fully eclipsed conformation
notes: The two CH₃ groups are directly eclipsed (dihedral 0°): the highest-energy conformation of butane (≈ 19 kJ/mol above anti) from torsional + steric strain.

molecules.name: Propane
notes: 10 σ bonds (2 C–C + 8 C–H); ∠C–C–C ≈ 112° (slightly more than 109.5° because of CH₃ repulsion).

molecules.name: Isobutane (2-methylpropane)
notes: Chain isomer of n-butane (same formula C₄H₁₀, branched skeleton). Branching lowers the boiling point: −11.7 °C vs −0.5 °C for n-butane.
Central C is bonded to three CH₃ groups and one H (a tertiary C–H).

molecules.name: Neopentane (2,2-dimethylpropane)
notes: Most branched isomer of pentane: nearly spherical, so weakest van der Waals forces and the lowest boiling point: 9.5 °C vs isopentane 28 °C and n-pentane 36 °C.
Central quaternary C has no hydrogens.

molecules.name: Cyclopropane
notes: C–C–C angle is forced to 60°, far from 109.5°: large angle strain (Baeyer strain, deviation 24°44′), and bent "banana" bonds. It is the most reactive cycloalkane.

molecules.name: Cyclohexane (chair)
notes: The chair conformation is strain-free: C–C–C ≈ 111° and all bonds staggered. Twelve H atoms are 6 axial (up/down) and 6 equatorial.
Boat and twist-boat forms are 30–45 kJ/mol less stable.

molecules.name: Ethene (ethylene)
notes: Both C are sp²: 5 σ bonds (1 C–C, 4 C–H) and 1 π bond. All six atoms lie in one plane, H–C–H ≈ 117°.
C=C 134 pm. The π bond (side-on overlap) prevents rotation, which is the origin of cis–trans isomerism.

molecules.name: Propene
notes: CH₂=CH–CH₃: two sp² carbons and one sp³ carbon; 8 σ + 1 π bonds. Markovnikov addition: H adds to the C bearing more H atoms.

molecules.name: 1,3-Butadiene
notes: Conjugated diene: the central C–C (146 pm) is shorter than a normal C–C (154 pm) because of π-electron delocalisation over all four carbons (sp²).
Planar s-trans form shown; it undergoes 1,2- and 1,4-addition.

molecules.name: Propadiene (allene)
molecules.shape: Linear C₃ skeleton; CH₂ planes perpendicular
notes: The central C is sp-hybridised (180° C=C=C); the two terminal CH₂ planes are at 90° to each other because the two π bonds use perpendicular p orbitals.

molecules.name: Ethyne (acetylene)
notes: Both C are sp: 3 σ bonds + 2 π bonds. Linear (180°), C≡C 120 pm, C–H 106 pm.
The sp C–H is the most acidic hydrocarbon C–H (pKa ≈ 25) because sp orbitals have 50% s-character.

molecules.name: cis-2-Butene
notes: Same groups on the same side of the C=C: (Z)-isomer. Geometrical isomerism arises from restricted rotation about C=C.
Polar (μ ≈ 0.3 D) and slightly higher boiling point (3.7 °C) than the trans isomer (0.9 °C), which is non-polar and more stable.

molecules.name: trans-2-Butene
notes: CH₃ groups on opposite sides of the C=C: (E)-isomer. Dipole moments of the two C–CH₃ bonds cancel, so it is non-polar and more stable than cis (less steric strain); it packs better, so its melting point is higher.

molecules.name: Benzene
notes: Planar regular hexagon: six sp² carbons, 12 σ bonds and 3 π bonds delocalised over the ring (6 π electrons = aromatic, Hückel 4n+2). All C–C are 139 pm (between 154 and 134).
Resonance energy ≈ 150 kJ/mol makes it much more stable than hypothetical cyclohexatriene; it does substitution (not addition) reactions.

molecules.name: Toluene (methylbenzene)
notes: CH₃ is an activating, ortho/para-directing group. Side-chain oxidation (KMnO₄) gives benzoic acid.

molecules.name: Phenol
notes: The O lone pair is delocalised into the ring (sp² O), so the C–O bond is shorter and phenol is far more acidic (pKa 10) than ethanol (pKa 16).
OH is a strongly activating, ortho/para-directing group; it gives a violet colour with neutral FeCl₃.

molecules.name: Aniline
notes: The N lone pair is partly delocalised into the ring (hence aniline is a weaker base than methylamine); NH₂ is activating and ortho/para-directing.
Gives the diazonium salt with HNO₂ at 0–5 °C.

molecules.name: Nitrobenzene
notes: The NO₂ group is planar with the ring; both N–O bonds are equal (resonance). It is a deactivating, meta-directing group.
Prepared by nitrating benzene with conc. HNO₃ + conc. H₂SO₄ (the nitronium ion NO₂⁺ is the electrophile).

molecules.name: Benzoic acid
notes: COOH is a deactivating, meta-directing group. Stronger acid (pKa 4.2) than acetic acid (4.76) because the sp² ring stabilises the carboxylate.

molecules.name: Chlorobenzene
notes: Cl is deactivating but ortho/para-directing. The C–Cl bond is stronger and shorter than in alkyl chlorides (partial double-bond character by resonance), so it resists nucleophilic substitution.

molecules.name: Naphthalene
notes: Two fused benzene rings: planar, 10 sp² carbons, 10 π electrons (aromatic). It sublimes easily (moth balls).
Resonance energy ≈ 255 kJ/mol. Substitution happens first at the α-position (C1).

molecules.name: Chloromethane (methyl chloride)
notes: Tetrahedral C; polar C–Cl bond (μ = 1.87 D). The simplest haloalkane; SN2 substrate.

molecules.name: Dichloromethane
notes: Dipole 1.60 D. Compare the methane series: CH₃Cl 1.87 D, CH₂Cl₂ 1.60 D, CHCl₃ 1.04 D, CCl₄ 0.

molecules.name: Chloroform (trichloromethane)
notes: Tetrahedral but unsymmetrical, so polar (1.04 D). Oxidised slowly by air/light to toxic phosgene (COCl₂), so it is stored in dark bottles.

molecules.name: Carbon tetrachloride
notes: Perfect tetrahedron (Cl–C–Cl = 109.5°): four polar C–Cl bonds cancel, so CCl₄ is NON-polar (μ = 0).
Not hydrolysed by water (no vacant orbital on C for attack).

molecules.name: Methanol
molecules.shape: Tetrahedral at C; bent at O
notes: O is sp³ with two lone pairs; C–O–H ≈ 108.5°, smaller than the C–O–C angle in ethers. Hydrogen bonding gives it a high boiling point (65 °C).

molecules.name: Ethanol
molecules.shape: Tetrahedral at C; bent at O
notes: Isomer of dimethyl ether (same formula C₂H₆O) but boils at 78 °C because of hydrogen bonding; dimethyl ether boils at −24 °C. A classic functional-group isomer pair.

molecules.name: Dimethyl ether
notes: C–O–C angle ≈ 111° (bigger than H–O–H in water because of the bulky CH₃ groups). No O–H, so no hydrogen bonding and a much lower boiling point than ethanol.

molecules.name: Diethyl ether
notes: An ether: sp³ O bonded to two ethyl groups, C–O–C ≈ 112°. Volatile, highly flammable solvent; forms explosive peroxides on standing.

molecules.name: Ethylene glycol (ethane-1,2-diol)
notes: A dihydric alcohol (two –OH): strong hydrogen bonding makes it viscous and gives a high boiling point (197 °C). Used as antifreeze.

molecules.name: Glycerol (propane-1,2,3-triol)
notes: A trihydric alcohol, viscous because of extensive hydrogen bonding. The backbone of fats and oils (triglycerides); nitrated to give nitroglycerine.

molecules.name: Methanal (formaldehyde)
notes: Planar: C is sp² (3 σ + 1 π), H–C–H ≈ 116°, H–C=O ≈ 122°. Polar C=O (μ = 2.33 D); the carbonyl C is electrophilic.
Aqueous solution (formalin, 40%) preserves biological specimens.

molecules.name: Ethanal (acetaldehyde)
notes: Carbonyl carbon is sp², CH₃ carbon sp³. Gives positive Tollens’, Fehling’s and iodoform tests.

molecules.name: Propanone (acetone)
notes: Simplest ketone: C=O carbon sp², C–C(=O)–C ≈ 116°. Highly polar (2.88 D). Gives the iodoform test (methyl ketone) but not Tollens’ or Fehling’s.

molecules.name: Methanoic acid (formic acid)
notes: Has both an aldehyde-like H–C=O and a carboxyl group, so it can reduce Tollens’ reagent. Strongest simple carboxylic acid (pKa 3.75).

molecules.name: Ethanoic acid (acetic acid)
notes: Carboxyl carbon is sp²; the carboxylate ion CH₃COO⁻ has two equal C–O bonds (resonance), which explains why carboxylic acids are much more acidic than alcohols.
Forms hydrogen-bonded dimers; vinegar is 5–8% acetic acid.

molecules.name: Ethyl ethanoate (ethyl acetate)
notes: An ester made from acetic acid and ethanol (Fischer esterification, with conc. H₂SO₄). Fruity smell; hydrolysed by acid or base (saponification).

molecules.name: Ethanamide (acetamide)
notes: The amide N lone pair is delocalised into C=O (resonance), so N is planar (sp²), the C–N bond is short, and amides are very weak bases. Hofmann bromamide reaction converts it to methylamine.

molecules.name: Urea (carbamide)
notes: First organic compound synthesised from an inorganic one (Wöhler, 1828: NH₄OCN → urea). Planar amide groups; 46% nitrogen, an important fertiliser.

molecules.name: Ethanenitrile (acetonitrile)
notes: The C≡N carbon is sp (linear C–C≡N, 180°), 2 π bonds. A strongly polar aprotic solvent (3.92 D). Hydrolyses to acetic acid.

molecules.name: Oxalic acid (ethanedioic acid)
notes: The simplest dicarboxylic acid; dibasic. Used as a primary standard in redox titration with KMnO₄ (5H₂C₂O₄ + 2MnO₄⁻ + 6H⁺ → 10CO₂ + 2Mn²⁺ + 8H₂O).

molecules.name: Methylamine
notes: N is sp³ with one lone pair (pyramidal); C–N–H ≈ 110°. A stronger base than ammonia in the gas phase and in water (alkyl groups push electrons to N).

molecules.name: Dimethylamine
notes: A secondary amine: N bonded to 2 C and 1 H, with one lone pair. Basic strength in water: (CH₃)₂NH > CH₃NH₂ > (CH₃)₃N > NH₃.

molecules.name: Trimethylamine
notes: A tertiary amine: no N–H bonds, so no hydrogen bonding between its molecules. C–N–C ≈ 111°. Smells of fish.

molecules.name: Glycine (zwitterion)
notes: In water and in the solid state amino acids exist as zwitterions: the –COOH gives H⁺ to –NH₂, so the molecule has both +NH₃ and COO⁻ and is neutral overall.
Glycine is the only achiral amino acid (its α-carbon bears two H atoms). It has high melting point and solubility like an ionic salt.

molecules.name: L-Alanine (zwitterion)
notes: A chiral α-amino acid with four different groups on the α-carbon. Natural proteins contain only L-amino acids (almost all with S configuration; cysteine is the exception).

molecules.name: (R)-Lactic acid
notes: Mirror image (enantiomer) of (S)-lactic acid. A chiral centre has four different groups: –H, –OH, –CH₃, –COOH. Enantiomers rotate plane-polarised light equally in opposite directions.

molecules.name: (S)-Lactic acid
notes: Found in sour milk and in muscle during exercise (L-(+)-lactic acid). Compare it with the R form: the two are non-superimposable mirror images.

molecules.name: α-D-Glucopyranose
notes: The cyclic six-membered (pyranose) chair form of glucose. In the α anomer the anomeric –OH (C1) is axial, trans to the CH₂OH group.
Anomers differ only at C1; they interconvert in water (mutarotation) through the open-chain form.

molecules.name: β-D-Glucopyranose
notes: In the β anomer the C1 –OH is equatorial, cis to the CH₂OH. All large groups equatorial makes β-D-glucose the most stable form (64% at equilibrium). Cellulose is a polymer of β-glucose; starch of α-glucose.

molecules.name: Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid)
notes: Analgesic, antipyretic and anti-platelet drug; made by acetylating salicylic acid with acetic anhydride. Contains an ester and a carboxylic acid on a benzene ring.

molecules.name: Paracetamol (acetaminophen)
notes: Antipyretic and mild analgesic (not anti-inflammatory); contains a phenolic –OH and an amide. Made by acetylating p-aminophenol.

molecules.name: Simple cubic (primitive) unit cell
notes: Each corner atom is shared by 8 cells, so Z = 8 × ⅛ = 1. Atoms touch along the cube edge: a = 2r.
Packing efficiency = (4/3 πr³) / (2r)³ = π/6 = 52.4 %, the lowest of the common cells; 47.6 % empty space.

molecules.name: Body-centred cubic (bcc) unit cell
notes: The body-diagonal is √3 a and carries 4r (corner–centre–corner), so r = √3a/4. Z = 8 × ⅛ + 1 = 2.
Packing efficiency = 2 × (4/3 πr³) / a³ = (√3 π/8) = 68 %.

facts.Examples: Na, K, Fe (α), Cr, W, Ba

molecules.name: Face-centred cubic (fcc / ccp) unit cell
notes: Atoms touch along the face diagonal (√2 a = 4r). This is cubic close packing (ABC ABC… layers).
Z = 4, so a unit cell has 4 octahedral and 8 tetrahedral voids (N and 2N for N atoms). Packing efficiency = 4 × (4/3 πr³) / a³ = π/(3√2) = 74 %.

facts.Examples: Cu, Ag, Au, Al, Ni, Pb

molecules.name: Hexagonal close-packed (hcp) unit cell
notes: Same 74 % efficiency and coordination number 12 as ccp, but layers repeat ABAB… (the 3 atoms in the middle sit in the hollows of the top and bottom layers).
Per hexagonal cell: 12 corner atoms × ⅙ + 2 face-centre atoms × ½ + 3 inside = 6.

molecules.name: Sodium chloride (rock salt) structure
molecules.shape: fcc of Cl⁻ with Na⁺ in ALL octahedral voids
notes: Cl⁻ ions form a face-centred cubic lattice; every octahedral void holds a Na⁺. Each ion has 6 nearest neighbours of opposite charge.
Z = 4: Cl⁻ = 8 × ⅛ + 6 × ½ = 4; Na⁺ = 12 edge atoms × ¼ + 1 body-centre = 4.

molecules.name: Caesium chloride structure
molecules.shape: simple cubic of Cl⁻ with Cs⁺ in the body-centre
notes: Not "body-centred cubic": the two ions are different, so the lattice is simple cubic with a two-ion basis. Z = 1.
The larger cation (r⁺/r⁻ ≥ 0.732) fits in the cubic void, giving 8 : 8 coordination.

molecules.name: Zinc blende (sphalerite, ZnS) structure
molecules.shape: ccp of S²⁻ with Zn²⁺ in ALTERNATE tetrahedral voids
notes: S²⁻ ions form fcc; Zn²⁺ occupies half (alternate) of the 8 tetrahedral voids. Each ion is tetrahedrally surrounded by 4 of the other kind.
Zinc blende has the same atomic arrangement as diamond, with two kinds of atom.

molecules.name: Fluorite (CaF₂) structure
molecules.shape: ccp of Ca²⁺ with F⁻ in ALL tetrahedral voids
notes: The larger-charged cation forms the fcc lattice (4 Ca²⁺); all 8 tetrahedral voids hold F⁻, giving a 1 : 2 ratio.
Coordination number: Ca²⁺ is surrounded by 8 F⁻ (cubic), each F⁻ by 4 Ca²⁺ (tetrahedral).

molecules.name: Antifluorite (Na₂O) structure
molecules.shape: ccp of O²⁻ with Na⁺ in ALL tetrahedral voids
notes: Antifluorite is the reverse of fluorite: the ANION forms the fcc lattice and the cations fill all tetrahedral voids (2 per anion), giving an M₂X formula.

molecules.name: Diamond (cubic unit cell)
molecules.shape: fcc of C with C in alternate tetrahedral voids
notes: Every C is sp³ bonded to 4 others in a tetrahedral 3D covalent network; hardest natural substance, electrical insulator, high thermal conductivity.
The unit cell has the zinc-blende arrangement with all atoms identical. Very open structure (packing efficiency only 34 %).

molecules.name: Graphite (two layers)
notes: Each C is sp² bonded to 3 others (C–C 142 pm) in flat hexagonal sheets; the fourth electron is delocalised over the layer, so graphite conducts electricity along the layers.
Layers (335 pm apart) are held only by weak van der Waals forces, so they slide over each other: graphite is soft, slippery and used as a lubricant and in pencils. Only two small patches are drawn.

molecules.name: Buckminsterfullerene
notes: 60 C atoms in 12 pentagons + 20 hexagons; every C is bonded to 3 others. There are 30 C=C double bonds (hexagon–hexagon edges) and 60 C–C single bonds (pentagon edges).
Discovered in 1985 by Kroto, Curl and Smalley (Nobel Prize 1996). A molecular solid that dissolves in benzene; each C is sp²-like with a fourth electron delocalised on the sphere.
